title: Edge-to-runtime contracts and team hand-offs
content:
TL;DR: This note captures a pragmatic decomposition of the surface between the edge/API gateway, the orchestration/control-plane, and runtime adapters (GPUs/hosts) across regions. Focus is on clear hand-offs, routing decision points, and a compact failure/fallback matrix so teams can own small, testable contracts instead of broad overlapping responsibilities.

Why this doc exists (context):
- Lots of emergent ambiguity in recent outages: teams debated where to perform model-version fallback, prefix-cache invalidation, and per-customer throttling.
- We need a small set of deterministic contracts to avoid cross-team hot-path coordination during incidents.
- Goal: each component has a crisp API and failure semantics; common failure modes have a default policy chain.

Audience: eng-platform-engineering, serving-runtime, infra, SRE, solutions-eng.

High-level principles (short):
- Keep routing decisions closest to the information they need (latency/cost/region) but keep policy declarative and centralized in the control-plane.
- Edge only makes fast, coarse decisions (auth, quota, region affinity). Complex falls/backoffs delegated to orchestration.
- Orchestration owns per-request policy evaluation and fallback planning; runtime adapters execute and surface granular telemetry and error types.
- Prefer explicit, testable fallthrough chains vs implicit heuristics.

Surface areas and contract sketches (simple):
1) API Gateway (edge) responsibilities:
- Authn/Authz (token validation, per-route ACL)
- Quota enforcement (fast path, local cache) with eventual reconciliation hook to control-plane
- Initial routing decision: map request to logical cluster (host pool) and preferred region using headers & routing table TTL.
- Provide request metadata to orchestration: client_id, model_id, model_version_hint, region_hint, latency_slo, cost_tier.
- Fast fallback: if upstream orchestration is unreachable, optionally return cached model-metadata or fail with 503 + Retry-After.
- Contract: edge accepts and forwards a standardized RoutingIntent proto (see linked confluence).

2) Control-plane / Orchestration responsibilities:
- Maintain authoritative routing policies and rollout state (model pins, canaries, weights).
- Evaluate per-request policy given RoutingIntent and live capacity metrics. Output: ExecutionPlan (primary adapter, fallback list, caching hints).
- Decision latency SLO: 50ms p95 for simple lookups; 200ms p95 for policy-eval with feature flags. If exceeded, return precomputed safe plan.
- Keep policy declarative: overflow rules, quantization preferences, and region affinity are data, not code.
- Expose a streaming watch API so edge can subscribe to critical plan changes.

3) Runtime Adapters (serving-runtime) responsibilities:
- Execute model generation as instructed by ExecutionPlan; return structured results and typed errors (CapacityExceeded, ModelMismatch, KVCacheMiss, InternalExecError).
- Report real-time metrics: offered QPS, queue depth, avg token latency, model-version actually used, quantization applied.
- Implement a minimal admission control surface: accept/delay/reject based on live GPU load.
- Provide a small control channel that allows orchestration to nudge (drain, pin-evict, health-check).

Routing decision points (where to act):
- Edge: quick coarse routing (region affinity, tier), local rate limiting, TTL-based cached plan.
- Orchestration: authoritative plan, fallbacks ordering, canary split, cache policies.
- Adapter: final arbiter for immediate admission/rejection; can trigger orchestration replan via async callback.

Failure & fallback matrix (compact):
- Adapter CapacityExceeded -> Orchestration: try next adapter in fallback list, possibly downgrade quantization; Edge notified for metrics.
- ModelMismatch (requested version not present) -> Adapter returns ModelMismatch error; Orchestration decides: (a) substitute compatible variant, (b) route to region with pinned model, or (c) fail with explicit user-facing error.
- Orchestration timeout -> Edge uses cached ExecutionPlan; if none, return 502 with clear Retry semantics.
- Edge lost connectivity to orchestration -> fail fast with cached plan; if policy TTL expired, degrade to global default: region-local, lowest-cost model variant.

Team ownership map (compact rows):
- API Edge (team: eng-gateway) — owns token lifetime, quota implementation, RoutingIntent emitter, health checks to orchestration. Oncall: eng-gateway pager.
- Orchestration/Control-plane (team: eng-orchestration) — owns policy store, plan engine, watch API, rollout tooling. Oncall: eng-orchestration pager.
- Serving Runtime / Adapters (team: eng-serving-runtime) — owns adapter SDK, typed errors, admission control hooks, per-host health. Oncall: eng-serving-runtime pager.
- Observability & Tracing (team: eng-observability) — owns trace schema, latency dashboards, token-level cost breakdown.
- Solutions & SRE (cross-team) — owns runbooks for cross-boundary incidents and customer-facing communications.

Operational playbook snippets (short):
- Incident: if "ModelMismatch" spikes, eng-serving-runtime owns initial triage; orchestration should stop any rollout touching the model, edge may put a short-lived block on routes.
- Capacity pressure: orchestration automatically promotes cheaper/quantized variants according to policy; if failures continue, edge will return 429 and circuit-break after threshold.

Migration notes (for teams implementing contracts):
- Phase 1: implement RoutingIntent emitter at edge and a passive orchestration stub that returns a safe default plan.
- Phase 2: runtime adapters emit typed errors and required metrics. Orchestration can then make smarter fallbacks.
- Phase 3: flip policy watch and rollback to final behavior; add automated canary experiments for fallback efficacy.

Small checklist for implementers: (keep short)
- [ ] Define RoutingIntent proto and ExecutionPlan JSON schema (backwards compatible).
- [ ] Orchestration watch API spec + SDK clients for Node/Python/Go.
- [ ] Adapter SDK: typed error enums and minimal admission control interface.
- [ ] Edge TTL semantics and reconciliation hook implemented.

Open questions / trade-offs (we should resolve soon):
- How much decision logic should live in edge vs orchestration for latency-sensitive routes? Tradeoff: pushing logic to edge reduces RTT but increases coordination complexity.
- Do we allow adapters to autonomously downgrade model precision, or must orchestration explicitly authorize?
- What is the canonical schema for "compatibility" across variants (embedding dims, output contract)?

Immediate next steps (owners & dates):
- Draft RoutingIntent/ExecutionPlan proto by 2025-03-10 (owner: Aisha Patel + Markus).
- Orchestration watch API PR (stub) by 2025-03-17 (owner: eng-orchestration).
- Adapter SDK typed errors by 2025-03-24 (owner: eng-serving-runtime).

Notes / random implementation tips (from field):
- Keep the fallback chain depth small — 2 fallbacks plus a degrade-to-error is easier to reason about.
- Use soft TTLs for cached plans so rollout changes propagate quickly but not noisily.
- Prefer explicit experiment flags for canaries and avoid implicit heuristics in adapters.

Appendix: quick examples (pseudo)
- RoutingIntent: {client_id: X, model_id: rmt-tiny-v2, requested_version: 3.1, latency_slo_ms: 150, region_hint: eu-west-1}
- ExecutionPlan: {primary: adapter://eu-west-1/pool-14, fallbacks: [adapter://eu-central-2/pool-2], quantize_hint: q8_0}
